📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the cheapest ways to fly Star Alliance business and first class.

Points for Business/First Class.

Picture this: you settle into a Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 business class seat on the upper deck, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, your fully flat bed already made up behind you. Fresh York to Frankfurt — a route that commands $4,000 to $8,000 in cash for a business class ticket — and you're here for 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles. No fuel surcharges. No carrier-imposed fees eating into your redemption. Just the experience. That's the moment the FI community lives for. Not the luxury itself — though Lufthansa's business class product is genuinely exceptional — but the *math*. The realization that the loyalty system has a pricing gap so wide you could fly a 747 through it. Here's what the numbers actually mean. At the low end, a $4,000 business class ticket redeemed for 63,000 points works out to **6.3 cents per point (CPP)**. At the high end — peak travel season, last-minute pricing, transatlantic demand — that same seat hits $8,000 in cash, which means your LifeMiles are delivering **12.7 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1–2 CPP a baseline for points value. You're achieving 6 to 12 times that baseline. The reason this feels like a genuine inefficiency rather than just a deal: Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards on a **fixed award chart** that doesn't fluctuate with cash fare demand. When airlines raise transatlantic business class fares during summer holidays or major events, your points cost stays exactly the same. The gap between what the market charges and what LifeMiles charges simply grows wider. And then there's the no-fuel-surcharge policy — the detail that separates LifeMiles from competitors like British Airways Avios, which can pile $600+ in carrier surcharges onto a single redemption. With LifeMiles, you pay government taxes only, typically $50–$150 for a transatlantic itinerary. That's it. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents exactly the kind of asymmetric value that underpins a great travel rewards strategy: use points where cash prices are highest, eliminate fees wherever possible, and fly a product you'd never justify paying full price for — because you didn't have to.

The core insight here is understanding why Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards so aggressively — and then understanding how to get points into the program swiftly enough to actually use them.

According to recent reports, avianca is a Star Alliance member, which means it has reciprocal award booking agreements with every other Star Alliance carrier — United, Lufthansa, Swiss, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines, and more. Like all alliance programs, LifeMiles can sell award seats on partner airlines. The pricing is set by Avianca's own award chart, not by Lufthansa's chart or United's chart.

This is the pricing inefficiency. Lufthansa's own frequent flyer program (Miles & More) charges over 100,000 miles for the same transatlantic business class route and layers on fuel surcharges. United MileagePlus charges 70,000–88,000 miles for the same seat. Avianca LifeMiles charges 63,000 miles with zero carrier surcharges. Same seat. Same plane. Wildly different cost.

Avianca keeps rates competitive because they want their program to be attractive to non-Avianca flyers — it's a revenue play. And because their route network is South America-focused, they've built a powerful award program that earns loyalty from customers who may never set foot on an Avianca plane.

It has been revealed that many programs claim no surcharges, then quietly pass through "carrier-imposed fees" that look indistinguishable from surcharges. LifeMiles is one of the genuine exceptions. On partner award bookings — including Lufthansa, Swiss, and other carriers that traditionally levy heavy surcharges — LifeMiles charges only government taxes. For a JFK–FRA business class award, expect to pay roughly $50–$150 out of pocket. That's the full cash outlay.

This is where the transfer partner ecosystem matters. LifeMiles accepts transfers from:.

Sources indicate that the instant Citi transfer is particularly powerful: if you find available award space today, you can move points and call LifeMiles to book within the same session. Capital One and Bilt are nearly as fast. Marriott's 3:1 ratio makes it less efficient unless you have a large Bonvoy balance and no better option.

LifeMiles runs frequent purchased miles sales, often 100%+ bonus miles on purchases. This is a legitimate strategy for topping off your balance when you're a few thousand miles short of a redemption. Combined with transfer partners, it creates significant flexibility. Watch for promotions at lifemiles.com — they typically appear 6–8 times per year.

It has been revealed that the golden rule of any points transfer: never transfer miles until you've confirmed award availability. LifeMiles miles are non-refundable once transferred, and award space can disappear in hours.

It has been revealed that united MileagePlus has one of the best Star Alliance partner award search tools available to the public. Go to united.com, start a search as if you're booking an award ticket, and look for business class availability on Lufthansa or Swiss flights on your target route. United displays Lufthansa partner space accurately in most cases. You're looking for "saver" level availability — marked as "X" class on Lufthansa.

Sources indicate that lufthansa's own website (lufthansa.com) sometimes indicates availability that United misses, and vice versa. Search both. You're not booking here — just confirming the seat exists.

An ExpertFlyer subscription ($10/month) lets you set availability alerts for specific routes and dates. For a high-value redemption like this, it's often worth one month of the service to monitor your target window.

LifeMiles opens its booking window 355 days in advance. For peak travel periods — summer transatlantic, major European events — set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Business class award space on Lufthansa releases in small batches and fills swiftly.

Transfer exactly what you need — 63,000 miles for a one-way business class transatlantic award — plus a small buffer of 2,000–3,000 miles for potential routing variations.

According to recent reports, go to lifemiles.com and search your award. The website has improved but can still be inconsistent with partner availability display. If the online search doesn't show the space you found on United.com, call LifeMiles directly at their customer service line. Have your flight numbers, dates, and cabin class ready. Phone agents can access and book partner availability that the website sometimes fails to display.

Industry observers note that after booking, you'll receive a confirmation email with a PNR (record locator). Verify this on the operating carrier's website — go to lufthansa.com or swiss.com and look up your reservation using the PNR. If it pulls up correctly, your booking is solid. Save this confirmation and check it once more 72 hours before departure.

It has been revealed that avianca LifeMiles uses a distance-based award chart for Star Alliance partner flights, and their chart is consistently 15-40% cheaper than competing programs for the same seats. The reason is strategic: Avianca wants to attract members to its loyalty program, and aggressive pricing on aspirational redemptions is how they compete with larger alliances. For you, this means the exact same Lufthansa First Class seat or ANA business class seat costs significantly fewer points when booked through LifeMiles versus through United MileagePlus or the carrier directly. The catch is that LifeMiles availability depends on the operating carrier releasing award space to partners, so you still need to search on the carrier or United.com before transferring.

Let's walk through a real redemption so you can see exactly what this looks like in practice.

The Route: Newly introduced York JFK → Frankfurt FRA, nonstop The Aircraft: Lufthansa Boeing 747-8, upper deck business class The Cash Price: $6,500 (a realistic peak-season transatlantic business class fare) The Points Cost: 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles Out-of-Pocket Fees: ~$85 in government taxes CPP Achieved: 10.3 cents per point.

You've transferred 63,000 Citi ThankYou points to LifeMiles — instantly — spotted the award space on United.com the morning it opened, called LifeMiles to confirm, and had your booking locked in within 90 minutes of finding the seat.

According to recent reports, lufthansa's 747-8 upper deck business class is one of the most iconic products in commercial aviation. The upper deck seats — in a 2-2-2 configuration — sit quieter and smoother than the main deck, with fewer passengers and a more intimate cabin feel.

According to recent reports, your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet. You'll have direct aisle access (depending on your seat selection), a large personal entertainment screen, and Lufthansa's catering, which consistently ranks among the top transatlantic carriers. The meal service on JFK–FRA is legitimate: a proper multi-course dinner, a breakfast service as you approach Germany, and a snack menu available throughout.

Before you board, you'll have access to Lufthansa's business class lounge at JFK — typically the Lufthansa Business Lounge or, depending on timing, the partner lounge. Hot food, showers, and a genuine departure experience that costs nothing beyond the taxes you've already paid.

The flight itself is roughly 7.5 hours. In a flat bed, that's a real night's sleep — or close enough. You arrive in Frankfurt rested, which matters whether you're connecting onward or starting your trip immediately.

For the ChooseFI community: this is the redemption that pays for the honeymoon, the milestone anniversary trip, or the family adventure you've been planning since you first discovered travel rewards. The $6,500 you didn't spend stays in your index funds.

According to recent reports, book at the 355-day mark for peak dates. Lufthansa releases a small number of partner award seats when the schedule opens. The travelers who get summer business class awards are almost always the ones who searched on day 355. Set a calendar alert. Be ready.

It has been revealed that use Citi ThankYou for time-sensitive bookings. Because Citi transfers to LifeMiles are instant, you can find award space and complete your booking in a single session. This matters when you're racing to secure a specific seat before someone else grabs it.

Industry observers note that watch for LifeMiles purchased miles promotions. If you're 10,000–15,000 miles short of a redemption, purchasing miles during a 100% bonus promotion can effectively cost you 0.5–0.7 cents per mile — still leaving you with excellent overall CPP on the redemption. Check lifemiles.com regularly or set a Google Alert for "LifeMiles promotion.".

Verify your booking on the operating carrier's website. After booking through LifeMiles, always look up your PNR on lufthansa.com or swiss.com. If it appears correctly, your seat is real. If it doesn't, call LifeMiles immediately.

Search Swiss as an alternative to Lufthansa. Swiss International Air Lines is also a Star Alliance member, also bookable through LifeMiles at the same rates, and also operates excellent business class products on transatlantic routes. Swiss often has more partner award availability than Lufthansa on certain dates.

Never transfer points before confirming availability. This is the most common — and most expensive — mistake in travel rewards. LifeMiles does not allow re-transfers out of the program.

Don't ignore the miles expiry policy. LifeMiles expire 12 months from your last earning activity. Any account activity — earning miles, purchasing miles, even a credit card transaction — resets the clock on your entire balance. Set a recurring reminder every 10 months to run a small transaction if you're holding a balance without an imminent booking.

Don't book Lufthansa First Class expecting the same experience. Lufthansa's First Class is a separate product with separate availability and pricing. Business class is the sweet spot here — outstanding value, more seats, and significantly better availability.

Avoid mixing Marriott Bonvoy® transfers with tight timelines. At 3:1 and 1–5 days transfer time, Bonvoy is the slowest and least efficient path into LifeMiles. Strategy accordingly.

It has been revealed that this redemption is built for the experienced FI traveler who has already earned their first free night or domestic flight and is ready to graduate to aspirational international business class. You don't need to fly business class constantly — but for a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or a long-planned European trip, this is the redemption that makes the experience extraordinary without derailing your savings rate.

This is NOT the right redemption if:.

According to recent reports, you need 63,000 LifeMiles per person, per direction. A couple flying one-way needs 126,000 miles. Most people will get there through a combination of one or two travel credit card welcome bonuses and organic spending — entirely achievable within the FI community's existing card strategy.

## Rated: Hard — Here's Why This redemption earns its **hard** rating from three compounding challenges, none of which is insurmountable but all of which require deliberate effort. **Challenge 1: Award Availability Is Limited.** Lufthansa releases partner award seats conservatively. You may search for weeks before finding space on your preferred route and dates. This isn't a redemption where you decide Tuesday you want to go and book Thursday. You need a booking window of weeks to months, and flexibility in your travel dates helps enormously. **Challenge 2: The Booking Process Has Friction.** LifeMiles' website doesn't always surface partner award availability accurately. You'll likely need to search on United.com to find the space, then call LifeMiles to actually book it. That phone call requires patience — hold times vary, and you'll need to clearly communicate flight numbers, dates, and cabin class to the agent. **Challenge 3: Timing the Transfer Is High-Stakes.** Because you can't transfer points *out* of LifeMiles, you're committing your points the moment you initiate a transfer. Finding the seat, moving the miles, and completing the booking requires confidence and speed. ## How to Overcome the Challenges 1. **Start searching early** — 300+ days out for peak travel. Use ExpertFlyer alerts to monitor availability passively. 2. **Use Citi ThankYou for instant transfers** so you can act immediately when you find a seat. 3. **Practice the phone booking process** once before your high-stakes redemption — call LifeMiles with a simple question to understand their system. If you've successfully booked one or two simpler awards before, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has members completing this redemption every year — and every single one says the boarding moment made the effort completely worth it.

Recent findings suggest that united demonstrates Star Alliance partner availability that LifeMiles can book. Search for Saver-level awards in business or first class on your target route. Note the exact carrier, flight number, and date.

Premium cabin award space is limited and competitive. Once your transferred miles appear in your LifeMiles account, complete the booking immediately. Do not wait — the seat can be taken by another searcher.

LifeMiles charges low taxes and fees on most partner awards, typically $30-$100 depending on the route. Some carriers (notably British Airways) add fuel surcharges, but most Star Alliance carriers keep fees minimal through LifeMiles.

Sources indicate that avianca LifeMiles is the program that lets FI-community travelers fly the same premium cabins as frequent business travelers at a fraction of the points cost. By consistently underpricing Star Alliance awards, LifeMiles turns 63,000-87,000 transferable points into experiences worth $8,000 or more. The process requires discipline (never transfer before confirming availability), patience (searching for saver space takes time), and a willingness to navigate a less polished booking experience. But the value is real: 15-20 cents per point on aspirational flights that would be unreachable at cash prices.

Pregnant or Raising a Baby? Medicaid or SNAP Already Meets WIC’s Income Rule

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you’re pregnant, recently pregnant, or raising a child under 5, WIC provides healthy food, infant formula, and breastfeeding help.
  • Only 32% of people on Medicaid who qualified for WIC were getting it in an average month of 2023, and 49% of eligible pregnant women, by USDA’s estimates.
  • Industry observers note that WIC’s income limit is 185% of the federal poverty line, and most states use USDA’s chart of the limit for each household size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you’re pregnant, recently pregnant, or raising a child under 5, WIC provides healthy food, infant formula, and breastfeeding help. In most states the income limit for a household of three is $50,542 a year before taxes, and Medicaid or SNAP enrollment qualifies you on income automatically. Apply through your local WIC office.

Only 32% of people on Medicaid who qualified for WIC were getting it in an average month of 2023, and 49% of eligible pregnant women, by USDA’s estimates.

Industry observers note that WIC’s income limit is 185% of the federal poverty line, and most states use USDA’s chart of the limit for each household size. If you get Medicaid, SNAP, or TANF cash aid, you qualify on income even with pay above the limit.

Take a couple earning $45,000 a year and expecting their first baby. As two people they’d be over the $40,034 limit, but the baby on the way can count as a third person, which puts them under the $50,542 limit for three. After the birth they’re still three, so the baby can get WIC for the first year, and the mother for six months, or the full year if she breastfeeds.

Industry observers note that WIC’s monthly benefit goes on an eWIC card, used like a debit card at WIC-approved stores and farmers markets. It buys set amounts of foods such as milk, eggs, produce, beans, and baby food, plus iron-fortified formula for babies who aren’t fully breastfed. Staff also offer nutrition counseling and breastfeeding help.

WIC pays only for those set foods, so for the rest of your household’s groceries, check whether you also qualify for SNAP.

Check whether you’re likely to qualify with USDA’s WIC Eligibility Tool, then contact your local WIC office by phone or online for an in-person or virtual appointment. Every applicant gets a free health check from WIC staff before enrolling. For the appointment, bring:.

Call your local WIC office as soon as you know you’re pregnant, since WIC can serve you through the whole pregnancy, not just after the birth.

#126311. Fire an Employee Legally – Warn in Writing First, Pay the Final Check on Time

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (490 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Fire an Employee Legally – Warn in Writing First, Pay the Final Check on Time

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • To fire an employee without inviting a discrimination or retaliation claim, document the performance or conduct problem and your written warnings as they happen, and decide on that record alone.
  • According to recent reports, outside Montana, most employees work at will, meaning you can let them go for any reason the law allows.
  • So the timing of a firing matters as much as its reason.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To fire an employee without inviting a discrimination or retaliation claim, document the performance or conduct problem and your written warnings as they happen, and decide on that record alone. Then let the employee go in a short private meeting, and pay the final check by your state’s deadline, which in some states is the same day.

According to recent reports, outside Montana, most employees work at will, meaning you can let them go for any reason the law allows. Every discrimination or retaliation claim argues that the real reason was one the law forbids, such as the employee’s race or a complaint they made.

So the timing of a firing matters as much as its reason. When it comes soon after the employee complained about discrimination or pay, asked for leave the law protects, or reported a violation, the timing itself can be evidence of retaliation. A written warning issued before any of those can show you would have fired them anyway.

According to recent reports, the final check is the other trap. No federal law requires paying a fired employee right away, but some states do.

Write up each problem when it happens, with the date, what went wrong, and what has to change, and give the employee a real chance to improve. Hold them to the same standard as everyone else, since excusing the same mistake in another employee can be enough to suggest a forbidden motive. For a firing that follows a recent complaint, offer severance pay in exchange for a signed release of the employee’s claims against you, and have an employment lawyer review it.

Picture a California restaurant owner whose server indicates up late three times in two months. She writes up each one, then fires the server in a five-minute private meeting with her manager as a witness. She takes back the keys, cuts off the server’s access to the scheduling app, and hands over the final check at the meeting, since California law makes all wages, unused vacation included, due the moment she fires someone.

Give the employee any unemployment notice your state requires. With 20 or more employees, also tell your health strategy within 30 days so it can offer continued coverage under COBRA, which applies to any firing short of gross misconduct.

Before you sit down with the employee, check your state’s final pay deadline with its labor office and have the check in hand.

#126310. Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

📅 13 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.
  • As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs.
  • But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time. Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

In a recent development, politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

But somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

This is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

So the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the….

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy.

1: The President Controls the Economy.

Recent findings suggest that if there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too big – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

Recent findings suggest that in reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

Industry observers note that the government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

2: The President Controls Interest Rates.

This one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

It has been revealed that the real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from newly introduced jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it).

According to recent reports, this line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

But most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR showed that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

4: The President Controls Housing Prices.

In a recent development, one crucial thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

Sources indicate that the dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, rapidly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are Right now “High” and We Want Them Lower.

Sources indicate that ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive).

Third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, fresh EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

Sources indicate that so why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About.

Sources indicate that the funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

It has been revealed that yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more promptly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

But have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

Recent findings suggest that and “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

According to recent reports, but alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

In the Comments: Has the election season been getting you down, pumping you up, or just giving you a thorough dose of “Meh”?

While researching economic stats for this article, I came across a quirky but informative series of videos called USA Facts by none other than former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. It seems that he had the same frustration as me: Americans are fighting over a bunch of opinions and misinformation without even bothering to look up the actual facts. So he made a well-produced series of videos that just share the facts without the baggage of political hype on top of them. I wish our politicians could do the same thing!

  • It has been revealed that both wordings come from the Federal Trade Commission’s care labeling rule, which lets a garment that can be washed or dry cleaned list just one of the two methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A “dry clean only” label warns that a garment can’t be washed, and the maker needs evidence to print it. Plain “dry clean” just names one safe way to clean the garment. Wash cotton, linen, and polyester pieces with that label at home, air and steam suits between cleanings, and ask your cleaner about bundle pricing for the rest.

Sources indicate that cleaners charged an average of $4.17 to launder a shirt and $18.89 to clean a two-piece suit in January 2026, according to a survey of 867 dry cleaners commissioned by Cleaner’s Supply. Sending out five shirts and a suit every week costs about $159 every four weeks at those prices.

It has been revealed that both wordings come from the Federal Trade Commission’s care labeling rule, which lets a garment that can be washed or dry cleaned list just one of the two methods. The fabric on the tag and the way the piece is built tell you which plain “dry clean” pieces you can wash yourself.

Cotton, linen, polyester, and cotton or acrylic knits wash well by hand or on a gentle cycle in cold water. Tailored suit jackets, silk, wool, leather, and rayon still belong at the cleaner, since water can shrink, spot, or misshape them.

Sources indicate that make each cleaning last longer, too. Let a wool suit hang on a wide hanger for at least a day between wearings, brush off lint, and blot spills right away. A handheld steamer takes out wrinkles between cleanings, and changing out of work clothes when you get home keeps dinner off them.

At the counter, ask whether the cleaner offers bundle pricing, a loyalty card, or a credit for hangers you bring back. For shirts you still send out, ask for the shirt price on a woman’s cotton button-down rather than the blouse price, which averaged $8.12 compared with $4.17 for a shirt. Paying more for the same job because a shirt is a woman’s is a pink tax.

Industry observers note that start with the shirts, which a cleaner washes in water just as your machine would. Washing those five shirts at home and having the suit cleaned every four weeks cuts that $159 to about $19, in exchange for one more load of laundry a week and the ironing.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A financial planner looks at your whole financial life, including insurance, taxes, and your estate, then hands you a blueprint.
  • The two overlap, and many firms sell both, so it’s easy to get pitched portfolio management when your real questions are about a budget, insurance, or buying a home.
  • According to recent reports, A planner answers questions that portfolio management doesn’t, such as how much life insurance to carry, whether to pay down debt or invest, and who should inherit what.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A financial planner looks at your whole financial life, including insurance, taxes, and your estate, then hands you a blueprint. An investment adviser manages your portfolio for a yearly percentage of it. Before you compare financial advisors, list the questions you want answered, and hire a planner if they go beyond investing and an adviser if they don’t.

The two overlap, and many firms sell both, so it’s easy to get pitched portfolio management when your real questions are about a budget, insurance, or buying a home.

According to recent reports, A planner answers questions that portfolio management doesn’t, such as how much life insurance to carry, whether to pay down debt or invest, and who should inherit what. Many planners charge for the initiative itself. In a 2024 Kitces Research survey of 621 financial advisors, the typical fee was $3,000 for a one-time plan, $300 an hour, or $4,500 a year for a retainer, a flat yearly fee for ongoing advice.

An investment adviser builds and runs your portfolio, usually for a yearly percentage of the money it manages. The same survey found a typical fee of 1% on balances up to $1 million. That fee rises with your balance, from $600 a year on $60,000 to $10,000 on $1 million.

Sources indicate that say you’re 35, with $60,000 invested and a new baby. Your questions are how much life insurance to buy, what your will should say, and how much to put in a 529 college savings plan. A one-time plan at the typical $3,000 answers all three. Paying 1% a year, about $600, for portfolio management alone answers none of them, so the $3,000 plan is the better buy.

Then match the help to where you are.

A single task, like filing a tax return or drafting a will, may call for a different kind of financial professional.

In each first meeting, ask for the fee in dollars at your balance and a written list of what it covers, and hire the firm whose list matches your questions.

Check your list against the best financial advisors to find firms that offer the help you need.

A romantic gift for your girlfriend or wife lands best when it shows you know her, and many of the most personal gifts cost little. Choose one drawn from your history together or her everyday life, and match it to the kind of partner she is.

Valentine’s shoppers keep spending more anyway. Those planning to celebrate in 2026 budgeted an average of $199.78 each for gifts, a record, and expected to spend $7 billion on jewelry, more than on any other category, by the National Retail Federation’s survey.

In a recent development, A gift’s price matters less than givers think. In a Stanford study published in 2009, givers expected recipients to appreciate a gift more the more it cost, since they took price as a sign of thought, but the recipients reported no such link.

It has been revealed that givers also misjudge sentimental gifts. In a 2017 study in the Journal of Consumer Psychology, givers chose between a gift matched to a recipient’s tastes and one tied to a loved one or a shared memory. They picked the first much more often than recipients wanted, and the researchers traced the gap to givers feeling less sure that the recipient would like the sentimental one.

Here are 10, each with its rough cost and the kind of partner it suits.

Every gift here works for a birthday or an anniversary as well as Valentine’s Day, and an anniversary can add a low-cost celebration that looks back on your years together.

It has been revealed that to choose, think about what she says she’s short on, whether that’s time to herself, a slow morning, or a reminder of your history together, and give her more of it. Then add a card with two lines on why you picked that gift for her.

Business class hops across Europe for fewer points than most domestic economy awards.

Picture this: you've just crossed the Atlantic on a long-haul award, touched down at London Heathrow, and now you need to get to Rome for the real adventure to begin. Most travelers at this point resign themselves to a cramped economy seat on a budget carrier, dragging luggage through a secondary terminal. But you? You're walking into the Virgin Atlantic clubhouse, sipping a Bloody Mary, and then settling into a proper business class seat for the 2.5-hour hop to Fiumicino. That's the magic of this redemption. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class seat on a short-haul European flight — London Heathrow to Rome, London to Athens, London to virtually any major European city — routinely retails for **$1,000 to $3,000 in cash**. Airlines know that business travelers on these routes are often on corporate accounts and will pay whatever it costs. The leisure traveler simply doesn't book business class on a two-hour flight because it feels absurd. And that's exactly the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community learns to exploit. Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club prices these short-haul European business class seats at a flat **17,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of that $1,000–$3,000 cash range, you're already extracting **5.7 cents per point** — well above what most programs deliver. At the high end, when those seats spike to $3,000 on peak travel dates, you're looking at a staggering **17.1 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. This one can deliver *ten times* that. What makes this feel particularly right for the FI mindset is the positioning angle. This isn't just a standalone splurge — it's the finishing move on a transatlantic trip you've already largely funded with points. You've landed in London. You need to get to your final European destination. Instead of paying $200 for a budget airline seat that charges extra for your carry-on, you drop 17,500 Virgin miles and arrive refreshed, fed, and ready. The opportunity cost of those miles is low; the experiential upgrade is enormous. This is what travel rewards done right looks like: not flying business class because you're wealthy, but because you understood the system better than the airlines expected you to.

The core insight here is understanding how Virgin Atlantic prices its own metal versus partner awards — and then deliberately choosing the right one for the right job.

According to recent reports, virgin Atlantic's Flying Club is famous in the points community for two things. First, its partner award sweet spots: ANA First Class for as low as 55,000–60,000 miles one-way, Delta One at competitive rates. These are the headline acts. But quietly sitting in the same award chart is a genuinely underappreciated gem — Virgin's own short-haul European business class, priced at a flat 17,500 miles regardless of the specific route within that distance band.

Sources indicate that why does Virgin price it this way? Virgin Atlantic operates as a premium carrier and sets its award chart to reflect aspirational redemptions — the kind that make Flying Club membership feel worthwhile. For long-haul routes on their own metal, their pricing is competitive but not exceptional. For short-haul Europe, however, the fixed pricing creates an opportunity: a two-hour flight to Rome or Athens costs the same 17,500 miles as a cheaper, shorter hop, but those premium routes have cash prices that routinely spike into the thousands. The chart wasn't built to be a loophole — it's just that cash prices for short-haul business class in Europe are genuinely volatile and often extraordinary.

The fuel surcharge reality check. Here's where you need to pay close attention. Virgin Atlantic is known for passing fuel surcharges onto award redemptions on their own flights. This is the opposite of what happens on ANA or Delta partner awards booked through Flying Club (which carry zero surcharges). On a short-haul European route, those surcharges are real but typically far more manageable than on a transatlantic segment — often in the $50–$150 range rather than $500+. The CPP math still works strongly in your favor, but you should go in with eyes open: this is not a zero-cash-outlay redemption.

The transfer path is exceptional. This is where the ChooseFI community has a serious structural advantage. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from essentially every major points currency:.

Every major transferable currency gets you there at a 1:1 ratio with instant speed. That means if you're holding Chase points from your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred, Amex points from your Gold or Platinum, or Citi points from your Premier card, you have a direct, frictionless pipeline to 17,500 Virgin miles within minutes of finding availability. This is critical because, as you'll learn in the booking section, Virgin availability on its own short-haul European routes can be limited, and you want to be able to move fast when a seat opens up.

Industry observers note that the booking window opens 331 days in advance — use it. Miles don't expire as long as you have account activity within 36 months, so there's no pressure to burn them before you're ready.

In a recent development, before you touch a single website, clarify your mission: you're looking for Virgin Atlantic-operated business class availability on short-haul European routes departing from London Heathrow (LHR). This is not a search for partner award space — this is VS metal, VS availability, VS seats. Your most common target routes will be LHR → FCO (Rome), LHR → ATH (Athens), and similar European city pairs. Build your itinerary around where VS actually flies in Europe, not every possible destination.

Recent findings suggest that go to virginatlantic.com and use the award search tool. Select "Book with miles" and enter your route. Virgin shows its own availability directly here — you don't need a third-party search engine for this specific redemption. Search one-way rather than round-trip so you can see each direction independently. If your target dates show no availability, flex by ±3 days. Business class award seats on short-haul routes are typically released in small batches.

Open a second browser tab and search the same route and date on Google Flights or directly on virginatlantic.com for a revenue ticket. Note the cash price for business class. This is your CPP sanity check — if the cash price is $1,200 and you're spending 17,500 miles plus ~$100 in surcharges, you're at roughly 6.3 cents per point. If the cash price is $2,500, your CPP jumps dramatically. This step helps you prioritize which dates to target.

Do NOT transfer points until you have confirmed award availability on your target date. Transfers to Virgin are one-directional and cannot be reversed.

Once you've confirmed a seat is available, transfer your points from your chosen program. For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers, the miles land in your Flying Club account instantly. Refresh your Flying Club account, confirm the miles are there, and complete the booking before the seat disappears. Enter your payment details for the taxes and surcharges (typically $50–$150 on short-haul European routes).

Virgin Atlantic operates its own short-haul flights from London Heathrow to destinations across Europe including Amsterdam, Paris, Edinburgh, Geneva, and Athens. These are different from partner codeshare flights. The 17,500-point price applies specifically to Virgin Atlantic-operated short-haul business class. Partner flights (booked through Flying Club but operated by Delta, KLM, or Air France) use a different award chart and typically cost significantly more. When searching, filter for Virgin Atlantic flight numbers (VS prefix) to find the sweet spot pricing. The business class product on short-haul includes a dedicated cabin, lounge access at Heathrow, priority boarding, and meal service.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is earned honestly. The difficulty isn't in the math or the concept; it's in three very real execution challenges. **Challenge 1: Finding award availability.** Virgin Atlantic doesn't release enormous quantities of business class award seats on its own short-haul European flights. You may search a dozen dates before finding a seat. This is the primary friction point. The fix: use the 331-day advance booking window religiously, and be genuinely flexible on your travel dates by at least ±3 days. **Challenge 2: Navigating the Virgin Atlantic booking interface.** Compared to programs like Chase's travel portal, Flying Club's award search tool is clunkier and less intuitive. It occasionally demonstrates availability that isn't actually bookable through to completion. The fix: search virginatlantic.com directly, be patient with the interface, and have your payment information ready to move quickly when a seat surfaces. **Challenge 3: Understanding the surcharge reality.** New points enthusiasts sometimes expect zero out-of-pocket on award bookings. Virgin's fuel surcharges on its own metal are real, and they'll surprise you if you're not expecting them. The fix: budget $50–$150 per person in cash costs as a baseline assumption. The good news: the **transfer path is as easy as it gets** in the points world. Instant 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt mean that once you find availability, you can have miles in your account and a booking confirmed in under 10 minutes. If you're willing to invest the search time and approach with patience, this is one of those redemptions that fundamentally changes how you see the travel rewards system. The payoff — business class in Europe for 17,500 miles — is worth the effort.

This redemption works best as part of a larger trip. If you are flying transatlantic to or from Europe, route through London Heathrow. Then use the short-haul award to connect to your final European destination at a fraction of the cost of a separate ticket.

According to recent reports, from its humble beginnings in 2008 to today, Bitcoin’s history has been relatively short but very eventful. The original protocol for this popular digital currency was created in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, believed to be a pseudonym for an unknown developer or group of developers.

Nakamoto launched the Bitcoin network just a year later and began mining the currency— an estimated 1 million bitcoins were mined in the early years.

The creator(s) of this first-of-its-kind asset developed the cryptocurrency in response to the Great Recession of 2007-2009, spurred by a distrust of the traditional banking system and concerns about its stability.

It has been revealed that given the recent values of Bitcoin, it’s hard to believe the currency first started trading on exchanges in 2010 at under $0.10. Since then, it’s experienced astronomical growth and some pretty wild price swings.

At its most recent high, one bitcoin was worth over $64,000—a far cry from trading for pennies in its earliest days.

Whether you’re thinking of investing in Bitcoin or you’ve held this cryptocurrency for several years, it’s fun to look back at this groundbreaking asset’s history. Read on for insights on Bitcoin milestones, historical returns, and how its returns compare to those of other assets.

#126279. Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1490 w)

Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1490 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.
  • “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
  • So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

I thought to myself at the time,.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

According to recent reports, among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

Industry observers note that with all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

Sources indicate that while my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

In a recent development, this level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

As we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

Sources indicate that in summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a fresh cost too since I was self-insured back then.

My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

It has been revealed that this strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

According to recent reports, first of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible blueprint ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze plan in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

But as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which indicates that,.

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

It has been revealed that for me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

In a recent development, the only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I currently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

But I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

According to recent reports, in the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

It has been revealed that but for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

A Temporary Note about Teslas and other electric cars:Rumor has it that the $7500 EV tax credit might be disappearing when our latest president takes over next week, so this might be the cheapest chance to buy what I feel are the best cars on the market: The Model Y, or Model 3.

Industry observers note that buy a money order where the fee is lowest, and pay with cash or a debit card. Before you leave the counter, fill in the name of whoever you’re paying, since only that person or business can cash it, and add your name, your address, and a memo. Keep the receipt until it’s cashed.

Walmart charges no more than $1 for a money order, while Chase charges $5 apiece on its Total Checking account.

Recent findings suggest that the post office charges $2.65 for a money order of up to $500 and $3.75 for one of more than $500. No postal money order can be for more than $1,000. Like Walmart, the post office takes cash or a debit card, and it refuses credit cards.

That makes Walmart the cheapest of the three, unless your landlord asks for postal money orders. Say your rent is $1,200 and your landlord does. Buy one for $1,000 and one for $200, and the fees come to $6.40 ($3.75 plus $2.65), while two $600 money orders would cost $7.50. For a payment that would take several money orders, ask your bank for a cashier’s check instead.

It has been revealed that the post office has you fill out a money order at the counter. Walmart tells buyers to bring their own details and those of the person they’re paying. Wherever you buy it, fill in these four things before you walk away:.

Then photograph each money order next to its receipt. Keep the receipts until your landlord cashes the money orders, since a receipt is how you track a payment or replace a lost one. If a postal money order goes missing, take its receipt to any post office to start a Money Order Inquiry, which can take up to 60 days, and a replacement costs $23.

Tech Report: Switch to a Safety Razor – Its Blades Cost Cents, Not Dollars

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A double-edge safety razor costs about $30 up front, but its blades cost about 15 cents each in a 100-pack, while name-brand cartridges cost dollars apiece.
  • The American Academy of Dermatology advises changing your blade every five to seven shaves, whatever razor you use.
  • Industry observers note that at $3.75 apiece, 52 of Gillette’s Fusion5 cartridges cost $195 a year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A double-edge safety razor costs about $30 up front, but its blades cost about 15 cents each in a 100-pack, while name-brand cartridges cost dollars apiece. Buy the razor and 100 blades, learn a light touch, and if you shave daily, they pay for themselves within a few months.

The American Academy of Dermatology advises changing your blade every five to seven shaves, whatever razor you use. Shave daily and change the blade every seventh shave, and you’ll go through 52 blades or cartridges a year.

Industry observers note that at $3.75 apiece, 52 of Gillette’s Fusion5 cartridges cost $195 a year. A $30 double-edge razor plus a $15 pack of 100 blades costs $45, enough for 100 blade changes, almost two years at that pace. The same 100 changes would cost $375 in cartridges instead of $45. By your 12th change, about three months in, the cartridges have already cost $45, as much as the razor and all 100 blades.

Shave your legs or underarms twice a week instead, and the payback takes more weeks but still comes by the 12th change. Any standard double-edge blade fits a modern double-edge razor, including one marketed to women, so one 100-pack can serve everyone in the house.

Recent findings suggest that the catch is a learning curve. Lather up, with a cream labeled for sensitive skin if yours is, then hold the razor so the blade meets your skin at about 30 degrees. Use short strokes in the direction your hair grows, press lightly to avoid nicks, and rinse the blade after each stroke.

Loose blades can’t go in a carry-on bag. TSA lets a safety razor through security only with the blade removed and asks that sharp items in checked bags be wrapped, so pack the blades that way. On carry-on-only trips, bring a cartridge razor, which TSA’s travel checklist permits.

At home, collect used blades in a metal tin with a slot or a lid, so they can’t cut anyone who handles your trash.

Blades differ in sharpness from brand to brand, so start with a sampler pack that holds blades from several brands, and buy 100 of the one that irritates your skin least.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.

Rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access.

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

Recent findings suggest that trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many users like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking.

Who it’s for: Users who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

PocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability.

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

Sources indicate that monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. People often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Users who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t want to link bank accounts, Bobby is a lightweight subscription tracker that lets you manually enter each subscription, along with billing dates and amounts. It then sends reminders so you don’t forget renewals. It’s simple, privacy-friendly, and great for a hands-on approach.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Who it’s for: Privacy-focused people or those who prefer full manual control.

In a recent development, subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android users. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.).

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android users.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:.

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

Here’s a quick guide based on what matters most to you:.

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and proposal better for annual vs monthly charges.

According to recent reports, subscription manager apps help plug the leaks in your financial bucket, so more of your hard-earned money stays where it belongs: with you. Whether you want automatic detection and help with cancellations, a full financial overview, or full privacy with manual entry, there’s an option that fits your style. Explore one or two subscription manager apps that align with your priorities, and don’t forget to check your finances regularly.

When I became an accredited investor, I found myself among an elite group with the financial means and regulatory clearance to access investments that many couldn’t. This opened doors to exclusive realms like hedge funds, venture capital firms, specific investment funds, private equity funds, and more.

Even though I had this “exclusive access” it took me a while to start investing in alternative asset classes.

The Securities and Exchange Commission states that as an accredited investor, I possess a level of sophistication that equips me to craft a riskier investment portfolio than a non-accredited investor. While this might not be universally true for everyone, in my case, I had demonstrated the financial resilience to bear more risk (see barbell investing), especially if my investments took an unforeseen downturn.

One of the intriguing aspects I discovered was that investment opportunities for accredited investors aren’t mandated to register with financial authorities. This means they often come with fewer disclosures and might not be as transparent as the registered securities available to the general public.

According to recent reports, an accredited investor is an individual or a business entity that is allowed to trade securities that may not be registered with financial authorities. They are entitled to this privileged access because they satisfy one or more requirements regarding income, net worth, asset size, governance status, or professional experience.

The concept of an accredited investor originated from the idea that individuals or entities with a higher financial acumen or more resources are better equipped to understand and bear the risks of certain investment opportunities.

Historically, the distinction between accredited and non-accredited investors was established to protect less experienced investors from potentially risky or less transparent investment opportunities.

Regulatory bodies, such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have set criteria to determine who qualifies as an accredited investor, ensuring that they have the financial stability and sophistication to engage in more complex investment ventures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, marriage usually helps your money through rights a live-in partner doesn’t get: a joint return that cuts taxes when one of you earns much more, spousal and survivor Social Security benefits, and inheritance without a will. Before you decide, figure your tax as a couple and as two singles, since two high earners can pay more tax once married.

Industry observers note that splitting rent saves money whether or not you marry. What marriage adds is legal rights, and for most couples they make it the better financial deal:.

Taxes cut both ways. Take a couple with no children who claim the standard deduction and earn $90,000 and $30,000 in wages. Under the IRS’s 2027 brackets, a joint return would lower their federal income tax by about $2,140 compared with two single returns, since more of the bigger salary is taxed at 12% instead of 22%.

In a recent development, one exception is two high earners. At $200,000 in wages each, they’d owe none of the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax filing single, but married they’d owe it on combined wages above $250,000, or $1,350 a year. They also share one cap on state and local tax deductions, and they reach the top 37% bracket at less than twice a single filer’s income.

In a recent development, staying single keeps every money decision yours, and no partner’s tax errors can cost you, since each spouse on a joint return owes the whole bill. Filing separately avoids that but generally costs more tax. A single parent filing as head of household can also owe more after marrying a partner who earns. You also skip a wedding, which averaged $34,200 for couples married in 2025, The Knot’s Real Weddings Study found. For most couples, these advantages are worth less than what marriage adds.

Before the wedding, total your tax on two single returns and on one joint return, since your marital status on December 31 decides how you file for the whole year.

Run both versions in one of the best free tax software programs.

Sources indicate that seven of the Bible’s money principles translate into habits you can start today: initiative before you spend, save for lean times, stay out of debt, spread your risk, grow wealth slowly, give generously, and be content. Pick the one your finances need most and put it to work this month.

Agreeing with these principles is the easy part. Living by them takes a habit concrete enough to start this week.

Industry observers note that most of the habits below can run on autopilot once you set them up, through an automatic transfer, a payroll deduction, or a recurring gift. Then you follow the principle every month without deciding again.

Each principle below comes with the verse behind it and one habit that puts it to work.

To find your starting point, look through last month’s bank and card statements. Pick the principle those statements show you following least, and set up its habit this week. For a household with no savings cushion, that’s Proverbs 21:20. With essential bills of $2,600 a month, an automatic $50 transfer to savings every Friday sets aside one month of bills in a year.

Before you buy or keep something you’d use only a few days a year, like a second car or camping gear, price renting or borrowing it instead. Add up a year of its insurance, storage, upkeep, and lost value, then compare that total with the cost of renting it for only the days you’d use it.

According to recent reports, you pay to own something every day of the year, however rarely you use it. A second car that leaves the driveway six weekends a year still needs insurance and registration for all 12 months.

In the sharing economy, apps and groups let people rent, borrow, or share things instead of owning them, so you pay only for the days you use something, or nothing at all.

Sources indicate that say a household owns a newly introduced, fully insured second car and drives it only on six weekend trips a year, 12 days in all. AAA’s 2026 figures put a new car’s yearly full-coverage insurance at $2,098 and its license, registration, and taxes at $802. That $2,900 alone comes to about $242 per day of driving, before gas or the car’s lost value. A car-sharing app that charges less than $242 a day, fees included, costs less than keeping the car. If transit and car sharing could cover your weekday trips too, run the same math on living without a car.

Sharing services come in three main kinds:.

For something you’d rather keep, neighbors in a Buy Nothing group give things away free.

Sources indicate that before booking a car, read the damage terms. Zipcar’s damage fee can reach $2,500 after an incident, and Turo’s protection looks aren’t insurance and don’t cap what you’d owe for interior or mechanical damage. Turo also charges a refundable deposit of $200 to $750 on some trips. Then read earlier renters’ reviews on the host’s listing.

Start with whatever you own that sat unused most of last year, and before you pay to insure or store it for another year, price renting it for only the days you used it.
