#126132. Roads Less Traveled

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1614 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Roads Less Traveled

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I explore some alternative routes through the mountains to finish my hike in Pennsylvania.
  • Sources indicate that as predicted, I was all set on sleep around 5:00AM.
  • Sources indicate that it didn’t take long to notice that my left leg was feeling a little goofy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I explore some alternative routes through the mountains to finish my hike in Pennsylvania. One works out well while the other does not.

Sources indicate that as predicted, I was all set on sleep around 5:00AM. Less predictable was the state of my left hip, which I had been sleeping on throughout most of the night and which was experiencing some discomfort. Counterintuitively, my “good” night of sleep with less waking during the night meant I spent too much time sleeping on one side of my body. Normally I wake up a handful of times and roll around to change my sleeping position. Time would tell if that would spill over into my hike. I opened my tent to hang up my water filter to get some water ready for breakfast and noticed that my interior mesh was ever so slightly damp. Indeed, the inside of my rain fly was wet. It hadn’t rained, I figured we must have had an unusually humid night. Not ideal. I was determined to get an early start on the day, I managed to have breakfast in my tent and get packing underway before sunrise. I scrambled onto Table Rock to watch the sun rise over Third Mountain. It was somewhere in the mid 30s this morning, with the humidity the cold was piercing through my shoulder-season apparel like it was barely there. Movement is the best cure so after snapping a few pictures of the sunrise I headed back to my tent, finished packing, and at 7:15AM was heading north on the trail eager to move Pennsylvania into the “Done” column.

Sources indicate that it didn’t take long to notice that my left leg was feeling a little goofy. There was a sensation in my hip that made me feel like I was stepping too narrow. I try swinging my leg around to loosen it up, but it didn’t help. My only choice was to hope it would go away once I warmed up.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

A darn good spot to camp for the night if I say so myself.

View of sunrise from Table Rock.

Recent findings suggest that last evening I studied the topographic map on FarOut and found that the gravel road between Second and Third Mountain is a viable alternative route back to my van. It would be roughly the same distance as the AT, but flatter and with less rocks, assuming gravel doesn’t count as rocks. I love a good alternate route that let’s me get a different perspective on my return leg so it felt like a no-brainer.

Recent findings suggest that the day began to slowly warm up as I hiked along Peters Mountain. By the time I was descending back into the valley the sun was shining directly on the south side of the ridge and providing plenty of warmth. Ahead was the climb up Third Mountain, knowing that I was about to get warm awfully I fast I stopped to shed my sleeping layers and load them into my pack. To connect to the gravel road, I needed to take the Knauber Trail up Third Mountain. It proved a tough, direct route up the mountain. The trail didn’t seem to get nearly as many visitors as the AT. There were leaves piled up several inches thick and I was having to heave myself up the trail with my trekking poles since my shoes were prone to slipping. I arrived at the crest of the ridge in a huff, and promptly felt the temperature drop now that I was between mountain ridges, out of the sun, and no longer climbing. My gloves went back on, and I decided to tough it out in my single layer sun hoodie rather than dig out my other layers.

Sunlight beams onto the trail toward Third Mountain.

Turning off onto the Knauber Trail.

The Knauber Trail proves to be a steep, leafy challenge.

In a recent development, the gravel road passed through a mountain gap and descended into the Stony Creek Valley. On the way, I passed an upright stone marker noting the spot where members of the Kabob Hiking Club have been gathering annually to commemorate the founding of their club. Apparently it began in 1934. This location is well off the beaten track. I suppose you could drive down the gravel road easily enough, but be prepared for a long drive.

Once the road settled between Second and Third Mountain it followed Stony Creek for what I imagine is somewhere between 8 and 10 miles. There are stretches of the road where you can see a full mile ahead, maybe more. It was honestly a little unsettling. Imagine hiking 10 minutes and the view ahead hardly looks any different. I found it more comforting to focus on the ground below me, at least that was moving. I enjoyed the steady progress, though there wasn’t much to see or report on, just pine trees and not a soul to be found.

The gravel road descends sharply to the Stony Creek Valley.

Yeesh that is a long, straight road.

Once I had made my way down the gravel road I took a moment to visit a few other markers at Rausch Creek. One sign explained the structures next to the creek were indeed filters as I had guessed yesterday. They use limestone to clean the water, which is why it looked so clear. I suspect the light gray color of the limestone settling on the bottom of the creek also helps the water to look brighter and more clear than if the creek bed were covered in natural rock.

As I made my way back toward Second Mountain I passed back through a flat section of trail that seems to flood regularly. Beavers had dammed some of the creeks and the soft soil caused many of the trees to fall, creating a relatively open area. Oddly, a plaid shirt was hung in the middle of the bog, one can only assume it belonged to one of the beaver’s victims.

In a recent development, with one final push I made my way up to Second Mountain where I made a miscalculation. High on the success of my gravel road alternate route, I decided to double down and take what appeared to be a shortcut. The AT crosses an abandoned dirt road which seemed to lead back toward the road not far from the trailhead where my van was parked. I found it odd that the road bent at a 90 degree angle just ahead on the map, but thought little of it. I forged along the road and did see a turn, but it was slightly too early to be the 90 degree turn on the map. Continuing on, the road continued straight ahead, which wasn’t shown on the map. There was also no 90 degree turn where it should have been. I decided to stick with the road that I was on even though I didn’t know exactly where it would go. Really, there were only two options, it would either end up near the road I was looking for, or it would turn a bit and eventually rejoin the AT.

In a recent development, it turned out to be the latter, albeit after some unwelcome elevation gain that meant I probably lost a bit of time by taking this route. My hip, which had gotten better after the first mile or so, acted up again around mile 20. It is a good thing I have a day off tomorrow for it to bounce back. It was nearly 4:00PM when I was back on the road making my way back to my van. I decided to use the afternoon to drive down to Hagerstown, Maryland so I could spend all day tomorrow focusing on tying up any remaining loose ends before starting off on my final section of the trail.

Entering the bog between Second and Third Mountains.

This is all that remains of the last hiker to trifled with the beavers.

Passing back through the meadow near Swatara Gap.

Total: 23.6 miles, 50,859 steps.

Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (318 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump.
  • In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food.
  • Sources indicate that it was too much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

Sources indicate that it was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

“They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” noted Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

According to recent reports, inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

It has been revealed that many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

#126130. Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2567 w)
📖 Baca

Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • It has been revealed that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • In a recent development, A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

It has been revealed that today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

In a recent development, A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Sources indicate that the main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

Leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

In a recent development, there are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data demonstrates him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

Recent findings suggest that his article, cryptically titled Among the Big Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Sources indicate that much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

According to recent reports, A recent study revealed that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

There is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper says that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

It has been revealed that there is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

His previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

According to recent reports, in a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

In a recent development, he continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

It would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Sources indicate that amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Recent findings suggest that clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

Sources indicate that as soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

In a recent development, the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

If he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

Industry observers note that in his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Industry observers note that the other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

The three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

Clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

Industry observers note that what exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

He had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

According to recent reports, clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

Sources indicate that if I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how massive they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

Recent findings suggest that his 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Sources indicate that clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

Industry observers note that in fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally said the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

It is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

One history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

The area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

According to recent reports, the line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

According to recent reports, I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary New Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

It has been revealed that the real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he reveals to the world.”.

#126129. The 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: General Information (Part 1)

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3434 w)

The 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: General Information (Part 1)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that each year, The Trek asks all Appalachian Trail hikers to complete a survey about their hike preparation, trail experiences, and personal backpacking journeys.
  • Our hope is that this survey serves as a great resource for prospective Appalachian Trail thru-hikers as they plan and prepare for their hike.
  • A note on the data: As this survey is intended to help prospective thru-hikers plan for the trail, we filter the responses to only include those who either initially planned to complete the entire trail or those who hiked enough on the trail to have pertinent statistics to thru-hikers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that each year, The Trek asks all Appalachian Trail hikers to complete a survey about their hike preparation, trail experiences, and personal backpacking journeys. We’ve taken all the information from our 293 responses this year and have analyzed it to help you better understand the Appalachian Trail Class of 2026.

Our hope is that this survey serves as a great resource for prospective Appalachian Trail thru-hikers as they plan and prepare for their hike. However, please keep in mind that no two hikes look the same, and you should by no means feel obligated to follow the trends or “averages” presented here. Use this data as a guide to inform your decisions, but remember that the most successful hike is the one that works best for you.

A note on the data: As this survey is intended to help prospective thru-hikers plan for the trail, we filter the responses to only include those who either initially planned to complete the entire trail or those who hiked enough on the trail to have pertinent statistics to thru-hikers.

We therefore excluded responses from hikers who hiked less than 500 miles and never intended to thru-hike; those who intended to complete an AT thru-hike but needed to stop before hiking 500 miles are still included. If you have any feedback on this benchmark, please leave a comment and let us know what you think the cutoff should be for 2027.

Sources indicate that using this framework, we have collected data from 294 AT long-distance hikers in 2026. The number will rise as we continue to accept responses from southbound hikers, and this survey will be updated with their information later into 2027.

This first post will focus on the broader demographics and logistics for Appalachian Trail hikers, while the next post will dig into the on-trail experiences and favorites/least favorites of this year’s Class.

AT Thru-Hiker Demographics Prior Experience, Injuries, and Completion Rates Direction, Start and Finish Dates, and Pace Budget.

Recent findings suggest that the age distribution of hikers starting the trail remains generally consistent year over year, though 2026 pushed the upper boundaries of the age range even further. This season, our youngest hiker was 16 years old, while at the other end of the spectrum, the oldest hiker was 76. (For comparison, the 2025 range spanned from 12 to 73, and 2024 ran from 18 to 71.).

Notably, though he did not fill out our survey, Dale “Grey Beard” Sanders was the oldest thru-hiker on trail this year, setting the age record for an Appalachian Trail thru-hike at 91.

We continue to see a large core group of hikers in their 20s and early 30s. These are typically recent college graduates and those unburdened by mortgage or family ties. This group is followed by another notable wave of hikers in their late 50s and early 60s, as retirees use their extra time and financial stability to take on the trail.

In a recent development, this year, the average age of an AT thru-hiker was 39, which remains much higher than the most commonly reported age of 25. In statistics, when the mean (39) sits well above the median (34) and mode (25), it points to a long tail end of older participants pulling the overall average upward.

READ NEXT: The Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey: All Years.

It has been revealed that since The Trek began collecting demographic data for the survey in 2016, the gender distribution has fluctuated between around 54 and 63% men. In 2025, 63% of survey respondents were men, which was the highest proportion of men to date.

This year, we stay consistent with that high proportion of men at 62.5%, while responses from women rose slightly to 34.8% and non-binary respondents held steady at just over 2%.

The trail remains overwhelmingly (96%) White, a trend that persists year over year as the proportion of White respondents has consistently landed above 90% since we began collecting demographic data in 2016.

While efforts to diversify the outdoors continue, the demographic data reveals that hikers identifying as White still make up the overwhelming majority, with fewer than 4% of hikers identifying as Hispanic, Asian, Black, Native American, or Pacific Islander. This number, while already small, is even smaller than in 2025, when we saw just over 4% of hikers identifying as non-White.

Industry observers note that as with previous years, the vast majority of survey respondents in 2026 (90%) were from the United States. Eleven other countries were represented among the respondents, which is slightly more than we saw last year, with international hikers primarily coming from Canada, the UK, and Germany.

Within the United States, the majority of hikers continued to hail from eastern and Mid-Atlantic states, taking advantage of closer geographic proximity to the trail.

As in previous years, we hypothesize that hikers from eastern states are more likely to tackle the AT due to easier travel logistics and greater familiarity and emotional connection with the area. Last year, Colorado marked the non-eastern state with the most respondents; this year, only 6 responses came from Colorado while Ohio and Texas each produced 10.

The states producing the most respondents this year were North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Virginia, tied for the top spot with 21 respondents each and closely followed by Georgia at 15 — all states found along the Appalachian Trail.

Education levels remained consistent with previous years — our survey indicates that Appalachian Trail thru-hikers continue to be a highly educated group, with two-thirds of respondents holding a Bachelor’s, graduate, or professional degree.

Similar to prior years, the small fraction of respondents indicating they did not finish high school is largely (though not entirely) accounted for by younger hikers who took on the trail as recent graduates or during gap periods.

This year, respondents hailed from over 200 distinct occupations before starting the trail. We’ve grouped them into the above categories, with STEM & Professional Services (Engineering, Technology, Science, Finance, Law, and Corporate Administration) once again leading the pack at 35.4% of responses.

Sources indicate that students and educators continue to make up a significant segment of the thru-hiking community. Educators alone account for 5.5% of respondents. When we asked participants how they secured the time off to thru-hike, 7.3% of respondents cited having summers off or seasonal flexibility, while another 6.9% leveraged scheduled breaks from school.

As in prior years, nearly 38.1% of respondents quit their jobs entirely to hike. Combined with the 23.2% who are retired, career breaks, transitions, and retirement make up over 60% of the total AT Class of 2026, showing how much a long-distance trail can stem from or cause a major life pivot.

The average hiker on the Appalachian Trail in 2026 had between one and seven nights of prior backpacking experience, with nearly 30% of respondents falling into the 1-to-3-nights bracket and over 21% falling into the 4-to-7-nights range. Very few respondents reported having no prior hiking or backpacking experience at all. Meanwhile, a strong group (13.3%) reported 3 months or more of prior experience, likely representing hikers who had previously completed other long-distance trails.

This year, we also examined the rates of unplanned early exits from trail across these prior experience levels. Interestingly, the data shows that prior backpacking experience does not strictly dictate success; hikers with modest experience (such as 1-3 nights or 4-7 nights) experienced relatively stable and moderate rates of not finishing (23% and 23.4%, respectively).

In a recent development, those with zero prior backpacking experience did face a higher-than-average attrition rate (31.6% for day hikers only and 50% for the two hikers who reported never hiking or camping, for what that tiny dataset is worth). Overall, though, the data continues to corroborate the idea that the Appalachian Trail can successfully be a first major thru-hike for well-prepared beginners.

This year, 73.9% of survey respondents completed thru-hikes with over 2,000 miles hiked, rebounding nicely from last year’s rate of 63.7% and surpassing the 71% mark reported in 2024.

In a recent development, however, this continues to trend much higher than the completion rates reported by the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC), which historically hovers around a 25% to 30% success rate. There are a few key reasons for this consistent disparity.

Industry observers note that first, the ATC captures a massive dataset of every registered start, whereas our survey relies on voluntary responses. Second, because we promote our survey through The Trek and our Instagram and community channels, we naturally attract responses from hikers who are plugged into the thru-hiking ecosystem and are often better equipped and more motivated to finish.

Sources indicate that we speculate that readers of The Trek are simply better prepared for the physical and mental demands of the trail after engaging with our guides and community. While we can’t prove that our content is the secret sauce to a successful AT thru-hike, please let us keep believing it for the sake of our ego.

Sources indicate that 75 survey respondents this year did not complete a full thru-hike. Of that group, 13.3% (10 hikers) said they only intended to hike a section or had already reached their personal mileage goal. That represents a sharp decline from 2025, when planned section hikers accounted for 39% of the non-finishing respondents (likely because we worked harder to filter out short-distance section hikers from the dataset this year).

When we look at the 65 hikers who experienced an unplanned exit from the trail, injury remains the undisputed primary reason, accounting for 38.7% of all non-finishers. Tying for the next most common reasons were family/personal obligations and mental burnout (such as boredom or loss of motivation), each accounting for 13.3% of respondents who left the trail.

Interestingly, while 2025 was an anomaly where zero respondents cited finances as their reason for leaving the trail, money troubles returned in 2026: running out of funds accounted for 8% of exits (6 hikers), tying with illness and the general physical toll of the trail.

In a recent development, one important note about this data: though we advertise this survey to the best of our ability, many hikers who unexpectedly left the trail early are likely not engaging with Appalachian Trail media by the time autumn rolls around. As a result, our responses remain skewed toward those who completed their hikes as planned, meaning we are likely only seeing a partial picture of trail attrition.

In a recent development, not only were injuries the largest cause of needing to leave the trail, but they were also quite pervasive among all the hikers on trail. More than half of our survey respondents (55.4%) experienced an injury during their 2026 hike, while 44.6% made it through unscathed.

Getting hurt on the Appalachian Trail does not automatically mean the end of the trail. Over 81% of injured hikers managed to stay on the trail by adapting their routine. Nearly a third of those injured (32.5%) hiked through the pain without taking any time off. Another 28.1% dialed back their daily mileage to recover, while 20.6% took some time off the trail.

Ultimately, 18.8% of reported injuries were hike-ending (9.9% of all respondents).

It has been revealed that in 2026, hike direction returned to its traditional pre-Hurricane Helene baseline, with the proportion of Northbound hikers jumping nearly 13 percentage points to 92.9% (up from 80.2% in 2025). Conversely, Flip-Flop hikes dropped from 13.5% to 5.0%, and Southbound respondents fell from 6.3% to 2.1%.

It has been revealed that that shift confirms last year’s spike in alternative itineraries was largely a temporary response to Hurricane Helene. Ahead of the 2025 season, the ATC and media outlets (like us!) encouraged hikers to pursue Southbound or Flip-Flop hikes to give southern trail towns and trail crews time to rebuild. With the southern portion of the trail recovered and reopened for the 2026 season, the vast majority of thru-hikers returned to the classic Georgia-to-Maine route.

Despite expectations last year that Southbound numbers would continue to climb as more people learned about the benefits of hiking south, the pull of the traditional Northbound social bubble remains hard to beat.

Most hikers began their hikes in March and April (accounting for nearly 75% of all start dates), with the single most popular start date this year shifting about two weeks earlier to March 14, closely followed by March 9.

Sources indicate that we asked respondents if they were satisfied with their start dates, and satisfaction jumped even higher this year: 94% of all respondents reported being happy with when they set out. Because the 2026 bubble shifted slightly earlier into March, the average start date for satisfied NOBO hikers moved up to March 18 (compared to March 29 in 2025).

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the average start date for NOBO hikers who felt they started too early was February 12, while the average date for those who felt they started too late fell between April 8 and April 10. With over 9 out of 10 hikers satisfied with their choice, the “right” start date ultimately comes down to the type of trail experience you want to have.

The small handful of hikers who felt they started too late cited weather concerns, wanting a slower pace during the first few weeks, not having enough time to heal from an injury and still finish, or feeling stressed as a solo hiker at the tail end of the bubble. Conversely, the five hikers who felt they started too early pointed to cold winter weather in February and early March. One April 6 starter noted they actually wished the trail had been more crowded.

If you want to start in what most thru-hikers consider the “sweet spot” for Northbounders, aim for a mid-to-late March window, keeping in mind that starting right in the March bubble means sharing shelters and campsites with bigger crowds early on.

Industry observers note that southbound hikers start later in the season — this year ranging from May 29 to August 12, with most setting out in late May and June — to let winter conditions clear up north. All eight of our current Southbound respondents reported being satisfied with their start dates, though the sample size remains too small to track broader date trends.

This year we’re keeping the survey open for Southbound applicants who are still on trail, and we’ll be back with more SOBO data early in 2027. SOBOs: click here to take the 2026 Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey.

Sources indicate that most successful thru-hikers finish between mid-July and mid-October, with September (86 hikers) and August (65 hikers) as the peak months for summiting Katahdin. The single most popular finish date this year was September 15 (9 hikers), closely followed by September 19 and August 26.

While a small handful of fast-moving Northbounders finished as early as late May and June — led by one early starter who wrapped up on May 31 and noted it was too early for weather-related reasons — the vast majority timed their finishes for late summer and early autumn, well within Baxter State Park’s typical May-to-October operating window.

It has been revealed that overall, 94.4% of thru-hikers reported being satisfied with their finish date. The average finish date that Northbound hikers were satisfied with was August 27 (shifting a little over two weeks later than last year’s August 11 average), while the average finish date reported as too late for weather-related reasons was September 10 for Northbounders. Two Northbound hikers who summited on September 19 and September 20 felt their finish dates were too crowded, landing right in the heart of the mid-September summit bubble.

With the information on start and end dates, we can look at the duration and pacing of hikers’ treks. We filtered this data to only include respondents who completed a thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail.

The average completed thru-hike this year took 160 days (just over five months), ticking up slightly from last year’s 153-day average. The longest reported thru-hike was 230 days (a flip-flopper who started February 27 and finished October 12), while the fastest completed thru-hike was an 88-day Southbound trek, followed closely by two Northbounders who finished in 96 days.

We also asked self-reported thru-hikers about their average daily mileage, with the overall average across respondents coming in at 15.0 miles per day (up from 14.3 miles per day in 2025). The single most-reported daily mileage was once again 15 miles per day (31 hikers), followed closely by 14 and 13 miles per day.

Recent findings suggest that even though our survey asks hikers to include zero days in their estimate, many respondents likely reported their hiking-day average rather than their true calendar average, or simply guessed without tracking exact daily numbers. Treat this figure as a loose ballpark: at the trail’s official length of 2,197.9 miles, the average 160-day thru-hike works out to a true calendar pace of roughly 13.7 miles per day once zero days and town stops are factored in.

Industry observers note that attendance at trail festivals rebounded strongly in 2026, driven by a return to classic Northbound traffic and high engagement among thru-hikers. While 44.2% of survey respondents still reported not attending any trail festival, that figure dropped significantly from 2025 (when 56% reported no festival attendance) as crowds returned to trail towns.

Trail Days in Damascus, Virginia remains by far the most popular AT festival, with 44.2% of respondents attending. Meanwhile, the Northbound Kickoff at Amicalola Falls saw a significant attendance bump, drawing 11.6% of respondents.

Unlike in prior years, we filtered our financial questions to include only those who completed their thru-hikes, to better reflect how much it actually costs to hike the entire trail.

Likely in part due to this decision, the average cost of an Appalachian Trail thru-hike (including the cost of gear) climbed notably this year to $8,863 (compared to $7,680 in 2025 and $7,602 in 2024), with a median spend of $8,500 and many hikers reporting total costs exceeding $10,000.

The spread of hikers across the cost spectrum highlights significant spikes around $6,000 and $8,000, along with 28 hikers reporting spending $10,000. At the extreme ends, only 6 hikers reported spending under $2,500, while 15 reported spending $15,000 or more.

Recent findings suggest that hikers spent an average of $2,305 on their gear in 2026 across all respondents who completed 500 miles or more on the AT, ticking up moderately from previous years. The median gear spend was $2,000, with the most common spending bracket also at $2,000 (57 hikers).

The vast majority of hikers spent under $4,000 on their gear, which covers the initial cost of purchasing packs, tents, and sleep systems along with the ongoing replacement or repair of footwear, clothing, and worn-out items over the course of their journey.

While most kept their setups budget-friendly or mid-tier with their spend peaking between $1,000 and $2,500, a few outliers scaled the high end of the luxury spectrum, with 11 respondents reporting gear investments exceeding $10,000 (including two hikers topping out at $11,000).

To those few hikers who absolutely splurged, shoot me a message. I’d love to know what on earth is in your pack.

We’re stopping here for now, but there is plenty more data to come. In the next few posts, we will break down everything from hiker experience levels and safety concerns to the nitty-gritty gear stats on shelters, footwear, and backpacks.

Sources indicate that looking for other years? Find every Trek AT thru-hiker survey on our Appalachian Trail Thru-Hiker Survey page.

#126128. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1384 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • Sources indicate that the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent new route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

Sources indicate that the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman mentioned. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two new routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

“The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he said.

He explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, major storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

The unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Industry observers note that “[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

In a recent development, one unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman claims this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Recent findings suggest that approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

In a recent development, “Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

“Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

According to recent reports, the team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

Sources indicate that the base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

Industry observers note that at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

That attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment complications, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he said.

In a recent development, in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

“However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he noted. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

It has been revealed that heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

Recent findings suggest that the summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

However, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

Recent findings suggest that route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

The trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to latest terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman stated.

Industry observers note that they then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

Descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Industry observers note that dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The new 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#126127. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1062 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • In a recent development, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

In a recent development, crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an key figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up aims for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

It has been revealed that as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

Though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Sources indicate that some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

Industry observers note that the caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

Industry observers note that the depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

It has been revealed that the main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

It has been revealed that attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

The high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and Fresh Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Sources indicate that despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” says Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

The columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

In a recent development, essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

In a recent development, according to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

As for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

According to recent reports, the arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

In terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

There have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • According to recent reports, “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

According to recent reports, “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

Recent findings suggest that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

It has been revealed that “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Recent findings suggest that baia notes the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no upcoming soft snow had accumulated.

Recent findings suggest that the Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

In a recent development, yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

Industry observers note that the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#126125. Breaking: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

Breaking: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing newly introduced route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • It has been revealed that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing newly introduced route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

It has been revealed that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin stated. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

Sources indicate that this was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” said Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

Industry observers note that for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he remarked.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

Sources indicate that if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Industry observers note that once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson remarked. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Sources indicate that thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” remarked Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

Sources indicate that that said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Recent findings suggest that buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Recent findings suggest that once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the significant cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

It has been revealed that to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

According to recent reports, “That is why it is key to consider all options and potential challenges before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

In a recent development, asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

According to recent reports, the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they said. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

In a recent development, they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles stated. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

According to recent reports, sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they said.

#126124. Causing a Scene: North Meets South on the AT
